newsitem.title: GERMANY: Iran trade delegation postpones German trip.
newsitem.headline: Iran trade delegation postpones German trip.

text.p: An Iranian trade delegation due to visit Germany next week to trawl for investment has postponed the trip, the German Chamber of Industry and Commerce (DIHT) said on Tuesday.

The move came amid a diplomatic row between Tehran and the European Union sparked by a Berlin court verdict last week which accused Iran's leaders of ordering the 1992 murder of four Kurdish dissidents.
The Iranian embassy in Bonn said the visit would "not be opportune at the present time", a DIHT spokesman said. The German Foreign Ministry declined comment on the decision.
Iran-experts in Germany said the postponement was by no means a sign of serious or lasting damage and that trade ties with Iran should get back to normal in a matter of weeks or months.
"The visit hasn't been cancelled. It's been postponed and if it can take place at a better time, we'll be pleased," said Michael Pfeiffer, head of the DIHT's foreign trade department.
"History proves that after such short periods of irritation, there are long periods of cooperation," Pfeiffer told Reuters.

The 26-strong trade delegation was due to visit Dresden, Hamburg and Bonn on a trip beginning next Monday aimed at seeking more German investment and marketing more Iranian products to one of Iran's biggest trading partners.
German experts said it was not an official delegation and the planned trip had been initiated by the Iranians.

Herbert Riedel, business manager of the German-Iranian chamber of trade in Hamburg, said it had been postponed partly over the politically charged atmosphere and partly because the delegation head was still recovering from a heart operation.

"I don't think the decision was influenced by events on the streets," Riedel said, referring to violent anti-German street protests in Tehran over the last few days and attempts by fundamentalist students to storm the German embassy complex.

"The visit was not to continue existing agreements, but aimed at promotion of Iranian products and to court more investment here," Riedel said. "I don't see it as a blow to trade. Things will largely get back to normal within weeks rather than months."

"The illness of Alinaghi Khamoushi played a role here. He is very important to the trip's success," Riedel said. He said Khamoushi, the president of Iran's Trade, Industry and Mining chamber of commerce, was recovering from a heart operation.
Iran expert Reinhard Schlaginweit from the German Foreign Policy Society was less optimistic about such a speedy recovery in trade ties, but agreed the lull was temporary.
"We must expect a rather cool period, but both sides have made it clear permanently damaged economic relations are not in their interests," Schlaginweit told Reuters.

"Trade will suffer and perhaps Iran will try to get bigger contracts from outside Europe, Japan for example. But I do expect a breakthrough (for ties with Germany and the EU) -- in a matter of months, not weeks."
The Berlin court ruled that Iranian leaders, including the state president and the religious leader, had ordered the killing of the Kurdish dissidents in a Berlin restaurant.
All EU members except Greece have recalled their top diplomats from Tehran for consultation and the bloc has suspended its policy of "critical dialogue" with Iran.
The policy aimed to keep communication channels with Iran open, encouraging pro-Western tendencies while not losing sight of issues of concern to the EU such as human rights.
Iranian leaders have sharply condemned the verdict and hundreds of thousands of people have demonstrated outside the German embassy in Tehran.
